meta.title: Payment Ledger
meta.summary: Move money between wallets and pay out to bank accounts with a double-entry ledger that never loses or invents a cent, even when requests retry and the provider times out.

functional: Pay out a wallet balance to the user's bank account through a payment provider
Show a wallet's balance and its full transaction history
Reject transfers and payouts that break balance, limit or fraud rules
Reconcile the ledger every day against the provider's settlement report
nonFunctional: Never lose, duplicate or invent money: every transaction's entries balance to zero
No wallet ever goes below zero
A retried request moves money at most once
Ledger entries are append-only and kept for 7 years for audit
Transfers respond in < 500 ms p99 with 99.95% availability

scale.label: Payouts
scale.value: ~2M per day (~25/s), mostly batched by the provider

scale.label: Ledger entries
scale.value: 2 per transfer ≈ 175M rows/day × ~150 B ≈ 26 GB/day before indexes

scale.label: Retention
scale.value: 7 years ≈ 65 TB of entries, partitioned by month

slos.name: Transfer availability
slos.sli: Transfer requests that return a definite answer (posted, or rejected by a rule) divided by all transfer requests, at the API gateway

slos.name: Transfer speed
slos.sli: Transfer requests answered within the threshold, divided by all transfer requests, at the API gateway

slos.name: Ledger always balances
slos.sli: Ledger transactions whose entries sum to zero per currency, divided by all transactions, checked continuously and in the nightly audit

slos.name: Provider movements reconciled
slos.sli: Provider settlement lines matched to a ledger payout within the threshold, divided by all settlement lines

alerts.when: Any transaction whose entries do not sum to zero, any wallet whose stored balance differs from the sum of its entries, or any wallet below zero
alerts.why: Money was created or destroyed by a bug. Freeze the affected accounts and stop the writer before more postings build on a wrong balance.

alerts.when: Transfer errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
Transfer errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak that would use up the month's budget in ten days.

alerts.when: Slow transfers burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Slow transfers make apps time out and retry, which adds load to the primary.

alerts.when: p99 row lock wait above 50 ms on any account for 15 minutes
alerts.why: A hot account (often a platform fee or provider cash account) serializes every posting that touches it, and transfers slow down before they fail.

alerts.when: Oldest unpublished outbox row older than 60 seconds
alerts.why: Balances are correct, but payouts and notifications wait behind the relay.

alerts.when: Payout submissions ending in a timeout or 5xx above 2% for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Each one parks a payout as UNKNOWN for reconciliation to settle. Users see slower payouts, but no money is at risk.

alerts.when: Unmatched settlement lines or ledger payouts older than 24 hours, or the nightly job not finished by 06:00 UTC
alerts.why: An unexplained difference between the ledger and the provider is either lost money or a ledger bug, and finance needs it explained before month end.

alerts.when: More than 500 payouts in UNKNOWN, or any older than 3 days
alerts.why: Users' money is stuck in clearing until reconciliation or support settles it.

alerts.when: Payout worker consumer lag above 10 minutes, or any event in its dead-letter topic
alerts.why: Payouts are not reaching the provider; the funds are safe in clearing but users wait.

alerts.when: Ledger read replica lag above 30 seconds for 10 minutes
alerts.why: History screens show stale balances, and reconciliation must wait for the replica to catch up.

signals.name: Lock wait per account
signals.why: Shows which account is hot before latency degrades for everyone.

signals.name: Idempotent replays and key conflicts
signals.why: A spike in replays means clients are timing out and retrying; mismatches mean a client is reusing keys for different requests.

signals.name: Outbox lag
signals.why: The age of the oldest committed event not yet on the stream.

signals.name: Payouts by status
signals.why: UNKNOWN payouts are the ones whose outcome only reconciliation can settle.

signals.name: Unmatched lines and amount
signals.why: Count alone hides a single large break; track the amount too.

signals.name: Decline rate by rule
signals.why: A sudden jump in one rule is either an attack or a bad rule change.

signals.name: Money moved
signals.why: The business view: a sudden drop in volume with no errors usually means a client or gateway problem.

signals.name: Idempotency keys stuck in started
signals.why: Each one is a request that crashed midway; a steady rise points at timeouts inside the posting path.

steps: Find the transaction ids the check flagged and read their entries: a missing leg or a wrong sign points at a code path.
Compare each affected wallet's stored balance with the sum of its entries to see whether the entries or the materialized balance is wrong.
Freeze writes to the affected accounts and find the deploy or migration that started it.
Fix forward with reversal and correcting entries, never by editing or deleting rows, and record why in the audit log.

debug.symptom: A user says a payout never reached their bank
steps: Look up the payout by id: status, provider reference and the ledger transactions linked to it.
If it is UNKNOWN or SUBMITTED, query the provider for that idempotency key and check whether a webhook was received and deduplicated.
Check the latest settlement report and the reconciliation result for that payout.
If the provider shows it paid, give the user the provider trace or bank reference; if it failed, confirm the reversal entries returned the funds to the wallet.

nodes.label: Wallet App
nodes.description: Creates one idempotency key per user action and reuses it on every retry

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the API hostname at the gateway

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Web ACL on the gateway: managed rules, bot control, rate rules; provider IP allowlist on the webhook path

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.description: TLS, user auth, rate limits; also the public endpoint for provider webhooks; reaches the service through a private integration (on AWS a REST API, the API Gateway type a web ACL can attach to)

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer
nodes.description: Private L7 load balancer in front of the Ledger Service fleet, with health checks across 3 zones

nodes.label: Ledger Service
nodes.description: The only writer of ledger tables: idempotency, balance checks, posting entries. Internal callers reach it through service discovery

nodes.label: Risk and Limits
nodes.description: Daily limits, velocity rules and fraud scoring before money moves

nodes.label: Velocity Counters
nodes.description: Per-user counters with TTLs: transfers per minute, amount per day

nodes.label: Ledger DB
nodes.description: accounts, transactions, entries (append-only), idempotency_keys, payouts, outbox

nodes.label: Ledger Read Replica
nodes.description: History, statements and reconciliation reads, kept off the primary

nodes.label: Outbox Relay
nodes.description: Publishes committed outbox rows to the event stream

nodes.label: Ledger Events
nodes.description: TransferPosted, PayoutRequested, PayoutPaid; keyed by account id so each account's events stay in order; a retry and a dead-letter topic per consumer

nodes.label: Payout Worker
nodes.description: Submits payouts to the provider through the NAT gateway, with the payout id as the idempotency key

nodes.label: Reconciliation Job
nodes.description: Nightly: matches the provider settlement report against ledger payouts

nodes.label: Settlement Files
nodes.description: Raw provider reports, write-once (object lock), kept 7 years

nodes.label: Payment Provider
nodes.description: Bank payouts (Stripe, Adyen, a bank API); sends signed webhooks

flows.title: Transfer between two wallets
flows.summary: Claim the idempotency key, check limits, then post two balanced entries, update both balances, store the response and write the outbox row in one database transaction.

steps.label: resolve api.wallet.example
steps.detail: The app finds the gateway by name. Resolvers cache the answer, so this is rare.

steps.label: gateway address
steps.payload: api.wallet.example.  60  IN  CNAME  d-7k2.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.

steps.label: POST /v1/transfers
steps.detail: The app generates the idempotency key once, when Alice taps Send, and reuses it on every retry. The amount is an integer in minor units (cents), never a float.
steps.payload:
POST /v1/transfers HTTP/2
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c9a2e-5b1d-4e8a-9c6f-0d2b4a8e1f37

{ "from": "acc_alice", "to": "acc_bob", "amount_minor": 2500, "currency": "USD", "memo": "dinner" }

steps.label: managed rules, bot + rate rules
steps.detail: The web ACL drops known exploit patterns, challenges scripted clients and caps requests per IP before the gateway spends any work, which blunts credential stuffing and card-testing style abuse of the money endpoints.

steps.label: allowed: forward
steps.detail: Only requests the web ACL allows reach the gateway.

steps.label: auth + rate limit
steps.detail: Checks the token belongs to the owner of acc_alice and caps requests per user, so a stolen token or a buggy client cannot hammer the ledger.

steps.label: create transfer (VPC Link)
steps.detail: The gateway reaches the private load balancer through a VPC Link, so the service is never on the internet. It starts the trace: traceparent goes with every hop and into the outbox event.
steps.payload:
POST /internal/transfers HTTP/1.1
traceparent: 00-6e0c63257de34c926f9efcd03927272e-4c721bf33e3caf8f-01
X-User-Id: u_alice
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c9a2e-5b1d-4e8a-9c6f-0d2b4a8e1f37

steps.label: to a healthy instance
steps.detail: Any healthy instance will do: the service is stateless and all state lives in the database. Instances failing health checks stop getting traffic.

steps.label: INSERT idempotency key
steps.detail: The primary key on (user, key) makes the claim atomic: exactly one request with this key gets the row. The request hash catches a client reusing a key for a different transfer. Keys are kept for 7 days, longer than any client retries.
steps.payload:
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (user_id, key, request_hash, status, created_at)
VALUES ('u_alice', '7f3c9a2e-...', 'sha256:91be...', 'started', now())
ON CONFLICT (user_id, key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING key;

steps.label: 1 row: new key
steps.detail: Zero rows would mean a retry of an earlier request: see the retry flow. A key stuck in started for over a minute (its first attempt crashed before posting) may be taken over by the retry, which is safe because nothing is posted without marking the key done in the same transaction.

steps.label: check 2500 USD acc_alice to acc_bob
steps.detail: Limits and fraud rules run before the posting transaction opens, so no row locks are held during a network call. If the risk service or its counters are down, transfers between wallets fall back to the hard limits checked in the ledger, and payouts wait (fail closed).

steps.label: INCRBY daily total
steps.detail: Velocity counters are approximate and expire on their own, which suits fraud signals. Hard limits that must be exact are checked against the ledger itself.
steps.payload:
MULTI
INCRBY spend:u_alice:2026-11-10 2500
EXPIRE spend:u_alice:2026-11-10 172800
INCR tx:u_alice:minute:1794312060
EXPIRE tx:u_alice:minute:1794312060 120
EXEC

steps.label: one transaction: entries, balances, outbox, response
steps.detail: Locking both accounts in id order prevents deadlocks, and the balance check under the lock prevents overdraft. Entries, balances, the outbox event and the stored response commit together or not at all; the unique idempotency key on transactions and the started guard on the key row mean a slow duplicate can never post twice.

steps.label: COMMIT
steps.detail: A deferred constraint trigger has checked that the debits equal the credits for tx_8841, and CHECK (balance_minor >= 0) on wallet accounts, before the commit succeeds.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.payload:
HTTP/2 201

{ "transaction_id": "tx_8841", "status": "posted", "balance_minor": 47500, "currency": "USD" }

steps.label: poll outbox
steps.detail: The relay only ever sees committed rows, so it can never announce a transfer that rolled back. Rows are split into a fixed number of slices by a hash of the key, and each relay instance owns some slices: work is shared, yet one account's events are always published in order by one relay.

steps.label: publish TransferPosted
steps.detail: Published at least once: if the relay crashes after publishing but before marking the row, the event goes out again, so consumers deduplicate by event id.

flows.title: Retried transfer replays the stored response
flows.summary: The first response was lost on a flaky mobile network. The retry carries the same key, finds the stored result, and no money moves a second time.

steps.label: POST /v1/transfers (retry)
steps.detail: The app timed out waiting for the answer, so it cannot know whether the transfer happened. It retries with the same key and body, after a backoff.

steps.label: allowed: forward
steps.detail: Retries pass the same web ACL; rate rules are set well above a normal app's retry pattern.

steps.label: INSERT key, then SELECT it
steps.detail: The insert finds the existing row, so this request is a repeat. Reading the stored row tells the service what the first attempt did.

steps.label: compare request hash
steps.detail: Same hash and done: replay the stored response. Different hash: 422, the key was reused for another request. Still started: 409, the first attempt is in flight, so retry later.

steps.label: 201 (replayed)
steps.detail: Byte for byte the original response, because it was saved in the same transaction as the entries. A new balance read here could differ and confuse the client.

flows.title: Payout to a bank, confirmed by webhook
flows.summary: Hold the funds in a clearing account first, call the provider in the background, and post the final entries when its signed webhook confirms the payout.

steps.label: POST /v1/payouts
steps.detail: Same idempotency contract as a transfer. The bank account was verified when it was added, and only its token is sent.

steps.label: create payout
steps.detail: The key is claimed exactly as in the transfer flow before anything else happens.

steps.label: check payout
steps.detail: Payouts are where stolen accounts cash out, so the rules are stricter: a new bank account, a recent password change or a payout far above the usual amount can hold it for review.

steps.label: move funds to payouts_in_flight
steps.detail: The money leaves the wallet now, into a clearing account, so Alice cannot spend it twice while the bank transfer is under way. The payout row is a mutable status record; the entries stay immutable.

steps.label: 202 Accepted
steps.detail: 202, not 200: the bank transfer takes minutes to days, so the API answers with a payout id the app can track rather than waiting on the provider.
steps.payload:
HTTP/2 202

{ "payout_id": "po_77", "status": "pending" }

steps.label: poll outbox
steps.detail: The PayoutRequested event exists if and only if the hold committed, so the worker can never pay out money that was not taken from the wallet.

steps.label: PayoutRequested po_77
steps.detail: The worker may receive the event twice. That is safe because the provider call below is keyed by the payout id.

steps.label: create payout, key = po_77
steps.detail: Using our payout id as the provider's idempotency key means any retry, from a timeout or a duplicate event, returns the same provider payout instead of sending money twice. The call leaves through the NAT gateway with an API key read from the secrets manager.

steps.label: pending, id tr_5Kq9
steps.payload: { "id": "tr_5Kq9", "status": "pending", "arrival_date": "2026-11-11" }

steps.label: mark SUBMITTED, ref tr_5Kq9
steps.detail: Only the status record changes. No entries are posted yet, because the money has not actually left the provider.

steps.label: UPDATE payouts SUBMITTED
steps.payload:
UPDATE payouts SET status = 'SUBMITTED', provider_ref = 'tr_5Kq9'
WHERE id = 'po_77' AND status = 'PENDING';

steps.label: POST /webhooks/provider payout.paid
steps.detail: Hours later the bank confirms, and the provider calls us. Providers deliver webhooks at least once and retry until they get a 2xx, so duplicates are normal.

steps.label: provider IP allowlist
steps.detail: A rule on /webhooks/provider only admits the provider's published address ranges. It cuts noise, but it is not the authentication: the signature check is.

steps.label: allowed: forward
steps.detail: Allowed through to the gateway's webhook route.

steps.label: forward webhook
steps.detail: The webhook route skips user auth; the signature check in the service is what authenticates it.

steps.label: verify signature + timestamp
steps.detail: An HMAC over the raw body with the shared secret (kept in the secrets manager) proves the provider sent it, and rejecting old timestamps stops a captured webhook from being replayed.

steps.label: dedupe event + post settlement
steps.detail: Recording the provider event id and posting the entries in one transaction makes the webhook idempotent: a duplicate inserts nothing and changes nothing. The settlement entries move the money out of clearing.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: Acknowledge duplicates with 200 too. Any other status makes the provider keep retrying for days.

flows.title: Payout times out, settled by reconciliation
flows.summary: The provider times out and the webhook never arrives. The money stays held in clearing until the nightly settlement report proves what happened.

steps.label: create payout, key = po_78
timeout after 10 s
steps.detail: A timeout is not a failure: the provider may have accepted the payout and the answer was lost. The outcome is unknown.

steps.label: back off 2 s, 8 s, 30 s with jitter
steps.detail: Retrying is safe only because the key is the same. Jitter keeps a fleet of workers from retrying in lockstep against a struggling provider.

steps.label: create payout, key = po_78 (again)
steps.detail: If the first call did reach the provider, it returns that payout rather than creating a second one.

steps.label: mark po_78 UNKNOWN
steps.detail: Do not refund the wallet: if the provider did pay, Alice would get the money twice. The funds stay in payouts_in_flight, where they are visible and accounted for.

steps.label: UPDATE payouts UNKNOWN
steps.detail: The same settle transaction the webhook uses. A unique constraint on (payout_id, kind) means that if the late webhook also arrives, only one of them posts: the other's insert fails and its whole transaction rolls back.

steps.label: GET settlement report 2026-11-09
steps.detail: At 02:00 UTC the job downloads the provider's report of every movement it settled that day, through the NAT gateway. This is the provider's book of record, independent of any webhook.
steps.payload: GET /v1/reports/settlements?date=2026-11-09&format=csv

steps.label: CSV, 1.9M lines
steps.payload:
provider_id,type,amount,currency,fee,reference,settled_at
tr_5Kq9,payout,10000,usd,25,po_77,2026-11-09T14:06:40Z
tr_7Hc2,payout,4200,usd,25,po_78,2026-11-09T16:12:03Z

steps.label: PUT raw file (object lock)
steps.detail: The untouched file is the evidence auditors ask for. Write-once storage means nobody can quietly edit it to make the numbers match. The job reaches the bucket through a VPC endpoint, not the internet.

steps.label: SELECT open payouts
steps.detail: Reading a replica keeps a heavy scan off the primary. A payout can settle days after it was created, so the query takes every payout not yet matched over the last 10 days, not just yesterday's. Seconds of replica lag do not matter for a closed day, and the resolve step below is idempotent anyway.
steps.payload:
SELECT p.id, p.status, p.amount_minor, p.currency, p.provider_ref
FROM payouts p
WHERE p.reconciled_at IS NULL AND p.status <> 'FAILED'
  AND p.created_at >= date '2026-11-09' - interval '10 days';

steps.label: match on payout id, compare amounts
steps.detail: Every line must match one payout with the same amount and currency, and the day's totals must agree; the provider's fee on each line is posted to the fee account as its own entries. po_78 is paid at the provider but UNKNOWN in the ledger, so it can be resolved automatically. Anything that cannot goes to a break queue for finance.

steps.label: settle po_78, source = reconciliation
steps.detail: The job goes through the Ledger Service instead of writing to the database, so every posting passes the same checks and leaves the same audit trail.

steps.label: post settlement entries
steps.detail: The same settle transaction the webhook uses. A unique constraint on (payout_id, kind) means that if the late webhook also arrives, only one of them posts.

notes.text: Money is an integer count of minor units (cents) plus a currency code, never a float: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in binary floating point, and a ledger must add up exactly. Each account holds one currency; a currency exchange is two balanced transactions through an FX account.

One relational primary with row locks gives the simplest strong guarantees: no overdraft, no lost update, atomic multi-row postings. The cost is a single write leader, which at 5,000 transfers/s peak (about 10 statements each) is the ceiling to watch; sharding is the next step (see the scaling question). Aurora keeps every commit in three zones, so a zone failure costs a failover that typically takes under a minute but no posted money. Locking the touched accounts in id order is cheaper than SERIALIZABLE isolation, which also works but aborts and retries more under contention.

Entries are append-only: the application role has INSERT and SELECT on entries but no UPDATE or DELETE, and mistakes are fixed with reversing entries. Each transaction can also store a hash of the previous one, so any tampering with history breaks the chain and the nightly audit finds it.

House accounts such as cash_at_provider and the fee account appear in a huge share of transactions and become lock hot spots. Split each into N sub-accounts chosen at random and sum them for reporting, or post to them in small batches. Partition entries by month so old partitions can be moved to cheaper storage.

A provider timeout leaves the payout outcome unknown. Retry with the same idempotency key (providers keep keys for a limited time, at least 24 hours for Stripe, so after that look the payout up by its reference instead of retrying), then park the payout as UNKNOWN with the funds still in clearing. Only a definite answer (a webhook, a status query, or the settlement report) may release the funds back to the wallet or move them out.

The outbox removes the dual-write problem: committing to the database and publishing to Kafka separately can fail halfway, but one transaction cannot. The relay is at least once, so every consumer deduplicates by event id; keying by account id, with one relay per outbox slice, keeps one account's events in order. A payout event that keeps failing goes to a dead-letter topic, and its funds stay safely in clearing.

The web ACL in front of the gateway runs managed rule sets, bot control and per-IP rate rules against credential stuffing and the scripted abuse money endpoints attract, and allowlists provider addresses on the webhook path. Secrets (the provider API key, the webhook signing secret, database credentials) live in the secrets manager, encrypted with KMS keys, and each is readable only by the one service that needs it.

questions.q: Why record each transfer as balanced debit and credit entries instead of just updating two balances?
questions.a: With double entry, every transaction's debits equal its credits, so money can only move and never appear or vanish, and a missing or wrong leg is caught by a simple sum. The entries are an append-only history from which any balance at any point in time can be rebuilt and audited. The stored balance is just a cache of the sum of entries, updated in the same transaction, and a nightly check proves they agree.

questions.q: Two transfers try to spend the last $25 in a wallet at the same moment. How do you prevent an overdraft?
questions.a: Do the balance check and the debit inside one transaction while holding a row lock on the account, for example SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a conditional UPDATE that only succeeds when the balance is high enough. The second transaction waits for the first, then sees the new balance and is rejected. Lock both accounts in a fixed order, such as by id, so two opposite transfers cannot deadlock.

questions.q: The app times out and retries a transfer. How do you guarantee the money moves only once?
questions.a: The client sends the same idempotency key on every retry, and the service claims it with a unique constraint before doing any work. The response is stored on the key row in the same transaction as the entries, so either both exist or neither does, and a retry replays the stored response. A key still in progress returns 409 (or is taken over if its first attempt died), and a key reused with a different body returns 422.

questions.q: The provider times out on a payout. Do you put the money back in the user's wallet?
questions.a: No, because the provider may have paid, and refunding would pay the user twice. Retry with the same idempotency key, query the payout status, and if still unsure mark it UNKNOWN with the funds held in a clearing account. A webhook or the next settlement report gives the definite answer, and only then do you post either settlement or reversal entries.

questions.q: Webhooks already tell you when payouts complete. Why also reconcile against the provider's settlement report?
questions.a: Webhooks can be lost, delayed or mishandled by a bug, and the provider can apply fees, returns or reversals you never heard about. The settlement report is the provider's own record of what moved, so matching it line by line against the ledger catches drift in both directions: money the provider moved that the ledger does not show, and ledger payouts the provider never made. Matches that cannot be explained go to a break queue for people to investigate.

questions.q: Write volume grows tenfold and one database primary can no longer keep up. How do you scale the ledger?
questions.a: First remove hot spots by splitting busy house accounts into sub-accounts, move history and reconciliation reads to replicas, and partition entries by time. Then shard by account id so most transfers stay inside one shard. A transfer that crosses shards becomes two local transactions through a clearing account, coordinated by an idempotent saga, or you move to a distributed SQL database such as Spanner that gives serializable transactions across shards.
